newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria agrees nuclear fuel supplies from Russia.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria agrees nuclear fuel supplies from Russia.

text.p: Bulgaria will pay Russia for nuclear fuel supplies in 1997 by selling electricity to its Balkan neighbours, Bulgarian Energy Minister Roumen Ovcharov said on Wednesday.

Ovcharov said his ministry had signed an agreement with Russia's first deputy nuclear energy minister Alexander Belosohov for fuel supplies next year for the Kozloduy plant, which are expected to cost some $50 million.

"We agreed to pay for the Russian nuclear fuel supplies through selling electricity to neighbouring countries including Turkey," Ovcharov told a news conference. Belosohov wound up a two-day visit to Sofia on Wednesday.
Ovcharov said Bulgaria signed a contract with Turkey for electricity exports on Wednesday. He declined to specify supply volumes.
Officials said Bulgaria could produce 40 billion kilowatt hours per year and could export up to three billion kilowatt hours per year.
Ovcharov said next week ministry experts will visit Russia to settle problems with transportation of nuclear fuel.
With the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Bulgaria needs special permission from Ukraine and Moldova to transport Russian nuclear fuel supplies through their territory.
Ovcharov said another Russian deputy energy minister was due to visit Sofia at the beginning of next year to discuss the problem of spent fuel disposal.
The former Soviet Union used to store spent fuel from the Kozloduy plant under an intergovernmental agreement which expired in 1990.

Ovcharov defended frequent energy price increases, saying that without them Bulgaria would face an energy catastrophe this winter and the energy sector might be one of the few in the country "which no longer entertains the illusion of socialism."

He said the scheme would prove its worth when a currency board regime was implemented next year, since state subsidies were excluded under the regime, which aims to introduce strict financial discipline.

National Electricity Company chairman Kozma Kuzmanov said Bulgaria was negotiating a Japanese credit for the construction of a new 920-megawatt coal-fired plant in the country's biggest mining and power complex Maritsa East One. The plant is expected to cost some $600 million.
Negotiations are underway for loans worth a total of $150 million for renovation of the Maritsa East Three plants and to connect Bulgaria to the European electricity network.
Bulgaria has also called a $250 million tender for the modernisation of the two most modern 1,000-megawatt reactors at Kozloduy.
